title: A ring-buffer event logger: a bounded queue

prereqs.why: This is the structure itself: an array, two indices, and a modulo that turns it into a circle.
The slots are a vector sized once in the constructor and then only ever written through, never grown.
Three files are compiled separately and linked, so a signature that does not match its declaration is a link error rather than a compile error.
Every index here is taken modulo the capacity, and the one that is not is the bug that reads past the end.

statement:
**Milestone 1 of 3.** A ring-buffer event logger, built one requirement at a time.
This milestone is the buffer itself: bounded, first in, first out.

### The files

```
ring_buffer.hpp   the interface. The public part is the contract; the
                  private part is yours to change.
ring_buffer.cpp   where you work. Every function is stubbed.
main.cpp          given, and read-only here: the command loop that
                  drives your buffer.
```

They are compiled separately and linked, the way a real build does it —
not pasted together. A diagnostic names the file it is in, and clicking it
opens that file at that line.

### The commands

The first line is the capacity. Every line after it is one command.

```
push <at> <text>   add an event; <at> is a whole number, <text> is one word
pop                remove and print the oldest event, or print `empty`
size               print `<held>/<capacity>`
dump               print every event held, oldest arrival first, or `(none)`
```

`push` prints nothing when it works. A command that is not one of these is
ignored, and so is a malformed one.

### What the buffer has to do

- It holds at most `capacity` events. `capacity` is at least 1.
- `push` adds the newest. When the buffer is **full** it refuses: it changes
  nothing and returns `false`, and the driver prints `full`.
- `pop` removes the **oldest** and hands it back. When the buffer is empty it
  returns `false` and the driver prints `empty`.
- `at(i)` is the i-th oldest event still held, so `at(0)` is the one `pop`
  would take next. It is only ever called with `i < size()`.
- Pushing and popping repeatedly must keep working: the storage is reused in
  a circle, which is the whole point of the structure.

### The sample

```
3                      capacity three
push 10 boot
push 20 login
size            ->     2/3
dump            ->     10 boot
                       20 login
```

### How it is checked

Your `ring_buffer.cpp` is compiled against the given `main.cpp` and run on
the cases. Any implementation that behaves as described passes — the slots
may be a `std::vector`, a `std::array`, a `std::deque` or anything else, and
the private members in the header are a suggestion you are free to replace.

This is one milestone of three. Your files are carried forward to the next
one, so what you write here is what you build on.
hints: Four of the seven functions are one line each. `size()` is the count you are keeping, `empty()` and `full()` are that count against nothing and against the capacity, and `capacity()` is already written. Get those right and the `size` command starts passing on its own.

Two indices do it: where the oldest event is, and how many there are. The newest one goes at `(start + count) % capacity` — which is one past the last, wrapped — and a pop moves `start` on by one, also wrapped. Nothing is ever shifted along.

`at(i)` is the same arithmetic as the push: the i-th oldest is at `(start_ + i) % cap_`. If `dump` prints the right events in the wrong order, that is the line to look at. If a refused push still changes the buffer, check that `push` returns before it touches anything.

cases.stdin:
3
push 10 boot
push 20 login
size
dump
pop
pop
pop
size

2
push 1 a
push 2 b
push 3 c
dump
pop
push 3 c
dump
cases.expect:
full
1 a
2 b
1 a
2 b
3 c
